newsitem.title: TURKEY: Court gives go ahead to key Turk Telekom sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Court gives go ahead to key Turk Telekom sell-off.

text.p: Turkey's constitutional court on Thursday approved the sale of Turk Telekom after three years of delay in a vote heralded as a possible jump start for the ailing economy.
The court rejected most of a challenge by 116 opposition MPs to the sell-off. "This decision will not block the sale of Telekom shares," a court official said.
Istanbul's stock exchange general index soared to an all-time high of 1,352 on the Telekom news, closing eight percent up on Wednesday.
Privatisation is the main pillar of ambitious targets to restore stability to Turkey's shaky finances.
"It is all about putting pieces into a jigsaw. This was a major piece," said Unal Kurtaran a Turkish equities analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.
The government hopes to raise $3.5 billion from the telecommunications sale, more than it has garnered in the last 10 years of privatisation efforts.
Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller predicted the Telekom ruling would remove doubts that were hanging over a further $5 billion worth of planned sell offs this year.
"With this decision by the constitutional court the way is opened for the rest of privatisation," she told reporters.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan said last week the 1996 budget deficit would be 1,200 trillion lira ($10.6 billion), compared with 316.6 trillion a year earlier.

Annual inflation, in double digits since the early 1970s, was 80 percent last year. But monthly figures in December that were lower than expected have pushed interest rates down to between 85-90 percent and extended maturities.
Brokers said the government's Telekom victory could help it meet a zero-deficit budget passed by parliament for 1997.
But they warned that lax tax collection, and a sieve-like social security system could gobble up some of the revenues gained.
"(The government) has been given a chance, if it can control the fiscal side, to balance the budget," said Volkan Sari of Global Securities in Istanbul.
Transport Minister Omer Barutcu told Reuters 10 percent of Telekom would be sold in the first tranche, due to be placed by the end of 1997.
"Ten percent will be issued to assess our market condition at that time," he said, noting that under the privatisation plan 49 percent of Telekom is to be sold.
A consortium headed by Goldman Sachs was appointed last month to advise on Telekom, the sale of which had been blocked by the constitutional court three times since 1993.
Premier Erbakan, an Islamist who had previously voiced opposition to interest rates under a Koranic ban on usury, had also been against privatisation.
But he appears to have been converted to the way of the free market by conservative partner Ciller since they formed an unlikely coalition last June.
Turkey has completed tenders for the sale of two banks, tyre, cement and ceramics plants and has leased port facilities in a spate of revenue-raising activity in the last five weeks.
"I give a big plus to the coalition for being persistent on privatisation," Salomon's Kurtaran said.
Some of the tenders have been broadcast live on television in a bid for transparency after charges of corruption marred previous sell offs.
A parliamentary probe last year cleared Ciller of illegally interfering with the privatisation of carmaker TOFAS to help business associates.
Two other graft accusations against her have been dropped with the Islamists' help, shoring up coalition unity.
